standard.title: Plate Tectonics
standard.description: investigate tectonic activity including the formation of geological features at divergent, convergent and transform plate boundaries and describe the scientific evidence for the theory of plate tectonics
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe properties and formation of sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic rocks and understand Earth's layered structure at a conceptual level (AC9S8U04 — same band). They have not yet examined plate boundary types, the geological features each produces, or the evidence base for the tectonic theory.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe geological features formed at divergent, convergent and transform plate boundaries, explain the forces driving plate movement, describe the scientific evidence that led to acceptance of plate tectonics over continental drift, and connect tectonic activity to hazard distribution and impacts on human populations.

nodes.label: The theory of plate tectonics and its evidence base
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the theory of plate tectonics — that Earth's lithosphere is divided into moving plates — and identify at least three distinct lines of evidence that supported its acceptance over earlier continental drift hypotheses.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the theory of plate tectonics and identify at least two lines of evidence that support it (e.g. continental fit, matching fossil records, mid-ocean ridge topography, earthquake and volcanic distribution).
nodes.typical_width: Students trace the development of evidence from Wegener's continental drift hypothesis to the acceptance of plate tectonics, identifying how each new line of evidence (seafloor spreading, seismic data, paleomagnetism, ocean floor topography) strengthened the theory — including the role of Marie Tharp's Atlantic floor maps.
wider: Construct a timeline of evidence that shows how the theory of plate tectonics was developed and accepted — examining why the initial continental drift hypothesis was rejected and what additional evidence was required
Research First Nations Australians' cultural accounts of earthquakes and volcanic events and explore how these long-term observational records contribute to understanding of tectonic history
Investigate how the extreme age and stability of the Australian craton relates to its plate tectonic history — examining why Australia experiences low tectonic activity compared to its neighbours
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat plate tectonics as a given fact rather than as an evidence-based theory cannot evaluate the geological features in Node 2 as evidence of plate movement — they list boundary features without understanding why those features confirm the theory. The evidence-reasoning framework established here is also required for the hazard-to-science-response reasoning at Node 3.

response_modes.reason: Students tend to treat plate tectonics as a given fact rather than as a theory that required accumulated evidence over decades to be accepted. The reasoning chain — initial hypothesis (continental fit) → rejected for lack of mechanism → new evidence types (seafloor spreading, seismics, paleomagnetism) → mechanism identified → theory accepted — is necessary to understand both the science content and the nature of scientific knowledge change (AC9S8H01).

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The evidence-development timeline and the story of Marie Tharp's contribution connect directly to AC9S8H01 (new evidence changes scientific knowledge) and AC9S8H02 (cultural perspectives influence science). First Nations geological knowledge provides a rich additional perspective on long-term observation of tectonic events.
success_criteria: Describes the theory of plate tectonics in terms of lithospheric plates and their movement
Identifies at least three lines of evidence supporting the theory and explains what each contributes

nodes.label: Plate boundary types produce distinct geological features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe what happens at divergent, convergent and transform plate boundaries and identify the geological features characteristic of each boundary type.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe one geological feature produced at each of the three boundary types (divergent, convergent, transform) and explain the plate movement that produces it.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the geological features produced at each boundary type — mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys (divergent), mountains/volcanic arcs/ocean trenches (convergent), fault lines (transform) — and explain the plate movement responsible. Students distinguish between oceanic-oceanic, oceanic-continental and continental-continental convergence and the different features each produces.
wider: Model interactions at different plate boundaries using physical materials or simulations — examining how the density difference between oceanic and continental crust determines which plate subducts
Investigate the relative significance of the driving forces of plate movement — slab pull, ridge push and mantle convection — and evaluate the evidence for each
Examine how the geography of the Asia-Pacific region reflects its position at active plate boundaries — connecting tectonic boundary types to specific regional geological features
nodes.hinge_reason: Boundary-type conflation — particularly applying subduction to all convergent boundaries regardless of crust type, or confusing divergent and transform features — produces systematic errors in Node 3 hazard distribution analysis. Students who cannot correctly attribute features to boundary types cannot explain why earthquakes and volcanoes are distributed where they are.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly conflate boundary types or apply 'subduction' to all boundaries. The three boundary types produce fundamentally different features via different mechanisms, and each type has sub-variants (convergent: oceanic-oceanic vs oceanic-continental vs continental-continental). Encountering multiple examples of each boundary type — with the features they produce — builds a more robust and accurate classification.

success_criteria: Describes one geological feature produced at each of the three boundary types with the plate movement responsible
Distinguishes between at least two types of convergent boundary and the different features each produces

nodes.label: Tectonic activity creates hazards and affects human populations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how tectonic activity at plate boundaries produces earthquakes and volcanic events, describe the distribution of these hazards in relation to plate boundaries, and examine engineering and scientific responses that support communities near active boundaries.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain why earthquakes and volcanoes are concentrated at plate boundaries and describe at least one engineering or scientific response that reduces risk for communities near active boundaries.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine patterns of earthquake and volcanic activity in relation to plate boundary types, evaluate the impact of tectonic events on human populations, and describe how scientific responses — improved prediction, early warning systems, earthquake-resistant building design — have reduced harm in countries near active boundaries.
wider: Investigate how seismic data is collected and shared between governments in the Asia-Pacific region and examine how this data is used for tsunami early warning systems — connecting tectonic science to international data sharing and policy (AC9S8H04)
Research how cultural building techniques (bamboo construction, traditional earthquake-resistant architecture) have influenced engineering solutions for earthquake-prone regions (AC9S8H02)

Examine how deep Earth imaging techniques (seismic tomography) have enabled identification of mineral, energy and water resources — connecting tectonic science to resource discovery and environmental considerations

response_modes.reason: Students often treat tectonic hazards as natural disasters without examining the role of science and engineering in managing risk. Varied regional contexts — Japan, Indonesia, New Zealand, the Pacific Ring of Fire — combined with examples of both prediction/engineering responses and their limitations, help students develop a more complete understanding of how tectonic science is applied in practice.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The seismic data sharing and tsunami warning direction (AC9S8H04) and the cultural building techniques direction (AC9S8H02) provide rich cross-strand connections. The resource discovery direction introduces a less obvious consequence of tectonic science that connects to mining and sustainability themes.
success_criteria: Explains why earthquakes and volcanoes are concentrated near plate boundaries using plate movement
Describes at least one scientific or engineering response that reduces risk for communities near active boundaries
Explains how scientific evidence is used to support communities living near active tectonic zones
